cnd19:2.1: Twice I asked the Sakyan: that brahmin asked the Buddha, the Blessed One, a question twice.
cnd19:2.3: “In the meantime this brahmin’s faculties will mature.”
cnd19:2.6: Or else, one who is wealthy, of great wealth, and possessed of riches is also a Sakyan.
cnd19:2.8: the wealth of faith, the wealth of ethics, the wealth of conscience, the wealth of prudence, the wealth of learning, the wealth of generosity, the wealth of wisdom, the wealth of the establishments of mindfulness, the wealth of right efforts, the wealth of the bases of psychic power, the wealth of the faculties, the wealth of the powers, the wealth of the awakening factors, the wealth of the path, the wealth of the fruit, the wealth of extinguishment.
cnd19:2.9: Because of these many kinds of treasures of wealth, one who is wealthy, of great wealth, and possessed of riches is also a Sakyan.
cnd19:2.10: Or else, one who is able, mighty, competent, brave, heroic, valiant, fearless, unflinching, unterrified, who does not flee, who has given up fear and terror, and who is free of any hair standing on end, is also a Sakyan.
cnd19:2.11: Twice I asked the Sakyan: twice I asked the Sakyan, I begged, I requested, I implored, I sought to win over—
cnd19:3.4: Mogharāja: this is the name of that brahmin … an expression—
cnd19:4.2: Did not answer me: he did not answer me, did not explain, did not teach, did not declare, did not establish, did not clarify, did not analyze, did not disclose, did not make known.
cnd19:4.3: Clear-eyed: the Blessed One is clear-eyed through five eyes—
cnd19:4.4: he is clear-eyed also through the eye of the flesh, clear-eyed also through the eye of clairvoyance, clear-eyed also through the eye of wisdom, clear-eyed also through the eye of a Buddha, clear-eyed also through the all-seeing eye.
cnd19:5.1: How is the Blessed One clear-eyed also through the eye of the flesh?
cnd19:5.2: In the Blessed One’s eye of the flesh five colors are found—
cnd19:5.3: a blue color, a yellow color, a red color, a black color, and a white color (…).
cnd19:5.4: Where the eyelashes are set, it is blue, deep blue, lovely, a delight to see, like a flax flower.
cnd19:5.5: Beyond that it is yellow, deep yellow, golden in color, lovely, a delight to see, like a champak flower.
cnd19:5.6: On both sides, the corners of the Blessed One’s eyes are red, deep red, lovely, a delight to see, like indagopaka beetles.
cnd19:5.7: In the middle it is black, deep black, not rough, glossy, lovely, a delight to see, like a fresh ariṭṭhaka fruit.
cnd19:5.8: Beyond that it is white, brilliant white, bright, clear white, lovely, a delight to see, like the morning star.
cnd19:5.9: With that natural eye of the flesh, which belongs to his bodily existence and was produced by past good conduct, the Blessed One sees a league all around, by day and by night.
cnd19:5.10: For whenever there is a darkness endowed with four factors, and the sun has set;
cnd19:5.11: and it is the sabbath in the dark fortnight, and there is a dense forest, and a great black cloud has risen up.
cnd19:5.12: In such a darkness endowed with four factors, he sees a league all around.
cnd19:5.13: There is no wall, door, rampart, mountain, thicket, or creeper that is an obstacle to seeing sights.
cnd19:5.14: If one were to mark a single sesame seed and drop it into a cartload of sesame, one could pick out that very seed.
cnd19:5.15: So pure is the natural eye of the flesh of the Blessed One.
cnd19:6.1: How is the Blessed One clear-eyed also through clairvoyance?
cnd19:6.2: With clairvoyance that is purified and surpasses the human, the Blessed One sees sentient beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly;
cnd19:6.3: in a good place or a bad place; he understands how sentient beings pass on according to their deeds—
cnd19:6.4: “These good beings were endowed with bad conduct of body, bad conduct of speech, and bad conduct of mind; they were slanderers of the noble ones, of wrong view, undertaking deeds based on wrong view. When their bodies broke up, after death, they were reborn in a place of loss, a bad place, the underworld, hell;
cnd19:6.5: but these good beings were endowed with good conduct of body, good conduct of speech, and good conduct of mind; they were not slanderers of the noble ones, of right view, undertaking deeds based on right view. When their bodies broke up, after death, they were reborn in a good place, a heavenly realm.”
cnd19:6.6: In this way, with clairvoyance that is purified and surpasses the human, he sees sentient beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, in a good place or a bad place; he understands how sentient beings pass on according to their deeds.
cnd19:6.7: And if he wishes, the Blessed One could see one world system, he could see two world systems, three world systems, four world systems, five world systems, ten world systems, twenty world systems, thirty world systems, forty world systems, fifty world systems, a hundred world systems; he could see a thousandfold lesser world system, a twice-thousandfold middling world system, a thrice-thousandfold world system, a great thousandfold world system; or as far as he wishes, so far he could see.
cnd19:6.9: In this way the Blessed One is clear-eyed also through clairvoyance.
cnd19:7.1: How is the Blessed One clear-eyed also through the eye of wisdom?
cnd19:7.2: The Blessed One is of great wisdom, of broad wisdom, of swift wisdom, of joyful wisdom, of keen wisdom, of penetrating wisdom; skilled in the analysis of wisdom, with analytic knowledge, having attained the analytical insights, having attained the four kinds of self-assurance, bearing the ten powers; a bull among men, a lion among men, a dragon among men, a thoroughbred among men, a yoke-bearer among men; of boundless knowledge, boundless splendor, boundless glory; wealthy, of great wealth, possessed of riches; a leader, a trainer, a guide, an instructor, a persuader, one who makes others see, and one who inspires confidence.
cnd19:7.3: For that Blessed One is one who gives rise to the unarisen path, who gives birth to the unborn path, who explains the unexplained path; he is the knower of the path, the discoverer of the path, the expert on the path; and now his disciples live following the path, becoming accomplished afterwards.
cnd19:8.1: For that Blessed One knows when he knows and sees when he sees; he has become the eye, has become knowledge, has become the teaching, has become Divinity; he is the speaker, the proclaimer, the one who draws out the meaning, the giver of the deathless, the lord of the teaching, the Realized One.
cnd19:8.2: For that Blessed One there is nothing unknown, unseen, uncomprehended, unrealized, or untouched by wisdom.
cnd19:8.3: Whether regarding the past, the future, or the present, all things come in every respect into the range of the knowledge of the Buddha, the Blessed One.
cnd19:8.4: Whatever is called knowable, to be known—whether the benefit of oneself, the benefit of others, or the benefit of both; benefit in this life or benefit in the next life; a meaning that is plain or a meaning that is deep; a meaning that is hidden or a meaning that is concealed; a meaning that needs to be interpreted or a meaning that has been drawn out; blameless benefit, benefit free of defilement, purifying benefit, or ultimate benefit—all of that revolves within the knowledge of a Buddha.
cnd19:9.1: All bodily deeds of the Buddha, the Blessed One, follow knowledge; all verbal deeds follow knowledge; all mental deeds follow knowledge.
cnd19:9.2: The knowledge of the Buddha, the Blessed One, is unimpeded regarding the past, unimpeded regarding the future, unimpeded regarding the present; as far as the knowable extends, so far extends knowledge; as far as knowledge extends, so far extends the knowable.
cnd19:9.3: Knowledge has the knowable as its limit, and the knowable has knowledge as its limit; knowledge does not proceed beyond the knowable, and beyond knowledge there is no path of the knowable.
cnd19:9.5: Just as, when two lids of a casket are perfectly joined, the lower lid does not extend beyond the upper, and the upper lid does not extend beyond the lower, but they stand as each other’s limit;
cnd19:9.6: in the same way the knowable and the knowledge of the Buddha, the Blessed One, stand as each other’s limit.
cnd19:9.7: As far as the knowable extends, so far extends knowledge; as far as knowledge extends, so far extends the knowable; knowledge has the knowable as its limit, and the knowable has knowledge as its limit.
cnd19:9.8: Knowledge does not proceed beyond the knowable, and beyond knowledge there is no path of the knowable.
cnd19:10.1: The knowledge of the Buddha, the Blessed One, operates in all things.
cnd19:10.2: All things are bound up with the Buddha, the Blessed One’s adverting, bound up with his wish, bound up with his attention, bound up with the arising of his mind.
cnd19:10.3: The knowledge of the Buddha, the Blessed One, operates in all sentient beings.
cnd19:10.4: The Blessed One knows the inclination of all sentient beings, he knows their underlying tendencies, he knows their temperament, he knows their dispositions; he knows sentient beings with little dust in their eyes and with much dust in their eyes, with keen faculties and with weak faculties, with good qualities and with bad qualities, easy to teach and hard to teach, capable and incapable.
cnd19:10.5: The world with its gods, Māras, and Divinities, the population with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans, revolves within the knowledge of a Buddha.
cnd19:11.1: Just as any fish and turtles, right up to the leviathan-gulper, revolve within the great ocean, in the same way the world with its gods, the world with its Māras, the world with its Divinities, the population with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans, revolves within the knowledge of a Buddha.
cnd19:12.1: Just as any birds, right up to the garuda Venateyya, revolve in a small region of the sky, in the same way even those who are endowed with wisdom like Sāriputta’s revolve in a region of the knowledge of a Buddha;
cnd19:12.2: the knowledge of a Buddha stands pervading and surpassing the wisdom of gods and humans.
cnd19:13.1: Even the wise among aristocrats, the wise among brahmins, the wise among householders, and the wise among ascetics—the subtle ones, skilled in the doctrines of others, like hair-splitting archers, who wander around, as it were, shattering views with their wisdom—having devised question after question, approach the Realized One and ask about what is hidden and concealed.
cnd19:13.2: Those questions are spoken about and answered by the Blessed One, and their reasons are made clear.
cnd19:13.3: And those people end up drawn in as followers of the Blessed One.
cnd19:14.1: How is the Blessed One clear-eyed also through the eye of a Buddha?
cnd19:14.2: Surveying the world with the eye of a Buddha, the Blessed One saw sentient beings with little dust in their eyes and with much dust in their eyes, with keen faculties and with weak faculties, with good qualities and with bad qualities, easy to teach and hard to teach, some of whom live seeing the danger of fault with regard to the other world.
cnd19:14.3: Suppose in a pond of blue water lilies, pink lotuses, or white lotuses, some blue water lilies, pink lotuses, or white lotuses are born in the water, grow in the water, do not rise above the water, and thrive submerged within; some blue water lilies, pink lotuses, or white lotuses are born in the water, grow in the water, and stand level with the water; and some blue water lilies, pink lotuses, or white lotuses are born in the water, grow in the water, rise up out of the water, and stand unsmeared by the water;
cnd19:14.4: in the same way, surveying the world with the eye of a Buddha, the Blessed One saw sentient beings with little dust in their eyes and with much dust in their eyes, with keen faculties and with weak faculties, with good qualities and with bad qualities, easy to teach and hard to teach, some of whom live seeing the danger of fault with regard to the other world.
cnd19:14.6: “This individual is of lustful temperament, this one is of hating temperament, this one is of deluded temperament, this one is of discursive temperament, this one is of faithful temperament, this one is of intelligent temperament.”
cnd19:14.7: For a person of lustful temperament, the Blessed One gives a talk on ugliness;
cnd19:14.8: for a person of hating temperament, the Blessed One teaches the development of love;
cnd19:14.9: for a person of deluded temperament, the Blessed One sets them in recitation, in asking questions, in listening to the teaching at the right time, in discussing the teaching at the right time, and in living with a teacher;
cnd19:14.10: for a person of discursive temperament, the Blessed One teaches mindfulness of breathing;
cnd19:14.11: for a person of faithful temperament, the Blessed One teaches an inspiring subject: the Buddha’s good awakening, the good teaching of the Dhamma, the good practice of the Saṅgha, and the precepts;
cnd19:14.12: for a person whose own temperament is intelligent, the Blessed One teaches a sign for insight: the aspect of impermanence, the aspect of suffering, the aspect of not-self.
cnd19:17.1: How is the Blessed One clear-eyed also through the all-seeing eye?
cnd19:17.2: The all-seeing eye is called the knowledge of omniscience.
cnd19:17.3: The Blessed One has reached, fully reached, approached, fully approached, is endowed with, fully endowed with, and possessed of the knowledge of omniscience.
cnd19:19.1: In this way the Blessed One is clear-eyed also through the all-seeing eye—
cnd19:20.1: I have heard that the divine seer answers when asked a third time: when asked a legitimate question up to the third time, the Buddha answers and does not put it off—
cnd19:20.2: so I learned it, so I retained it, so I took note of it.
cnd19:20.5: Just as kings who have gone forth are called royal seers, and brahmins who have gone forth are called brahmin seers, in just the same way he is both the Blessed One and a seer—
cnd19:21.1: Or else, the Blessed One is also a seer because he has gone forth.
cnd19:21.2: He is also a seer because he has sought, searched for, and looked for the great aggregate of ethics.
cnd19:21.6: He is also a seer because he has sought, searched for, and looked for the great aggregate of knowledge and vision of freedom.
cnd19:21.7: He is also a seer because he has sought, searched for, and looked for the tearing apart of the great mass of darkness.
cnd19:21.8: He is also a seer because he has sought, searched for, and looked for the breaking up of the great perversion.
cnd19:21.18: He is also a seer because he has sought, searched for, and looked for the raising of the great banner of the teaching.
cnd19:21.25: He is also a seer because he has sought, searched for, and looked for the great ultimate goal, the deathless extinguishment.
cnd19:21.26: Or he is sought, searched for, and looked for by beings of great power—
cnd19:21.27: “Where is the Buddha, where is the Blessed One, where is the god of gods, where is the bull of men?” and for that reason too he is a seer—
cnd19:21.28: I have heard that the divine seer answers when asked a third time.
cnd19:24.3: The other world: excluding the human world, every other world is the other world—
cnd19:25.1: The realm of Divinity with its gods: the world with its gods, Māras, and Divinities, the population with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans—
cnd19:26.1: They do not know your view: the world does not know your view, your approval, your preference, your belief, your inclination, or your intention—
cnd19:26.2: “This one has such a view, such an approval, such a preference, such a belief, such an inclination, such an intention”—they do not know, do not see, do not perceive, do not grasp, do not find, and do not obtain—
cnd19:27.1: Of the renowned Gotama: the Blessed One has attained fame, so he is renowned.
cnd19:27.2: Or else, the Blessed One is honored, respected, esteemed, revered, and venerated, and he receives robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicines and supplies for the sick, and for this reason too he is renowned—
cnd19:30.1: The one of excellent vision: one of excellent vision, one of foremost vision, one of best vision, one of outstanding vision, one of leading vision, one of highest vision, one of ultimate vision—
cnd19:31.1: I have come seeking with a question: I have come needing something by means of a question …
cnd19:31.2: Carry this burden: in this way too, I have come seeking with a question.
cnd19:32.1: How to look upon the world: how, looking upon the world, reviewing it, weighing it, assessing it, clarifying it, and making it evident—
cnd19:33.1: The King of Death does not see: the King of Death does not see, does not perceive, does not reach, does not find, does not obtain—
cnd19:36.2: World: the world of hell, the world of animals, the world of ghosts, the human world, the world of gods, the world of the aggregates, the world of the elements, the world of the sense fields, this world, the other world, the realm of Divinity with its gods.
cnd19:36.5: In what way, sir, is it called the world?”
cnd19:36.6: “It wears away, mendicant, and so it is called the world.
cnd19:36.8: The eye wears away, mendicant, sights wear away, eye consciousness wears away, eye contact wears away, and the pleasant, painful, or neutral feeling that arises dependent on eye contact also wears away;
cnd19:36.12: the mind wears away, ideas wear away, mind consciousness wears away, mind contact wears away; and the pleasant, painful, or neutral feeling that arises dependent on mind contact also wears away.
cnd19:36.13: It wears away, mendicant, and so it is called the world.”
cnd19:37.1: Look upon the world as empty: he looks upon the world as empty for two reasons—
cnd19:37.2: either by recognizing that its course is beyond control, or by observing that choices are vacuous.
cnd19:37.3: How does he look upon the world as empty by recognizing that its course is beyond control?
cnd19:37.4: No control is found over form, no control is found over feeling, no control is found over perception, no control is found over choices, no control is found over consciousness.
cnd19:37.7: For if form were self, mendicants, this form would not lead to affliction, and one could compel form—
cnd19:37.8: ‘May my form be like this, may my form not be like that.’
cnd19:37.9: But because form is not-self, mendicants, form leads to affliction, and one cannot compel form—
cnd19:37.10: ‘May my form be like this, may my form not be like that.’
cnd19:38.2: For if feeling were self, mendicants, this feeling would not lead to affliction, and one could compel feeling—
cnd19:38.3: ‘May my feeling be like this, may my feeling not be like that.’
cnd19:38.4: But because feeling is not-self, mendicants, feeling leads to affliction, and one cannot compel feeling—
cnd19:38.5: ‘May my feeling be like this, may my feeling not be like that.’
cnd19:39.2: For if perception were self, mendicants, this perception would not lead to affliction, and one could compel perception—
cnd19:39.3: ‘May my perception be like this, may my perception not be like that.’
cnd19:39.4: But because perception is not-self, mendicants, perception leads to affliction, and one cannot compel perception—
cnd19:39.5: ‘May my perception be like this, may my perception not be like that.’
cnd19:40.2: For if choices were self, mendicants, these choices would not lead to affliction, and one could compel choices—
cnd19:40.3: ‘May my choices be like this, may my choices not be like that.’
cnd19:40.4: But because choices are not-self, mendicants, choices lead to affliction, and one cannot compel choices—
cnd19:40.5: ‘May my choices be like this, may my choices not be like that.’
cnd19:41.2: For if consciousness were self, mendicants, this consciousness would not lead to affliction, and one could compel consciousness—
cnd19:41.3: ‘May my consciousness be like this, may my consciousness not be like that.’
cnd19:41.4: But because consciousness is not-self, mendicants, consciousness leads to affliction, and one cannot compel consciousness—
cnd19:41.5: ‘May my consciousness be like this, may my consciousness not be like that.’”
cnd19:42.2: “This body, mendicants, does not belong to you, nor to others.
cnd19:42.3: This is an old deed, mendicants, to be seen as shaped by choices, as intended, as something to be felt.
cnd19:42.4: There, mendicants, the learned noble disciple attends carefully and rationally to dependent origination itself—
cnd19:42.5: ‘Thus, when this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises;
cnd19:42.6: when this does not exist, that does not come to be; with the cessation of this, that ceases; that is—
cnd19:42.7: ignorance is a condition for choices, choices are a condition for consciousness, consciousness is a condition for name and form, name and form are a condition for the six sense fields, the six sense fields are a condition for contact, contact is a condition for feeling, feeling is a condition for craving, craving is a condition for grasping, grasping is a condition for continued existence, continued existence is a condition for rebirth, rebirth is a condition for old age and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress to come to be—
cnd19:42.8: that is how this entire mass of suffering originates.’
cnd19:43.1: But when ignorance fades away and ceases with nothing left over, choices cease; when choices cease, consciousness ceases …
cnd19:43.2: with the cessation of rebirth, old age and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress cease. That is how this entire mass of suffering ceases.”
cnd19:43.3: In this way he looks upon the world as empty by recognizing that its course is beyond control.
cnd19:44.1: How does he look upon the world as empty by observing that choices are vacuous?
cnd19:44.2: No essence is found in form, no essence is found in feeling, no essence is found in perception, no essence is found in choices, no essence is found in consciousness;
cnd19:44.3: form is without essence, insubstantial, bereft of essence, whether by way of the core essence of permanence, of pleasure, or of self, or by way of what is permanent, stable, eternal, or not liable to change.
cnd19:44.7: consciousness is without essence, insubstantial, bereft of essence, whether by way of the core essence of permanence, of pleasure, or of self, or by way of what is permanent, stable, eternal, or not liable to change.
cnd19:45.1: Just as a reed is without essence, insubstantial, bereft of essence, and just as a castor-oil plant …
cnd19:45.2: and just as a cluster fig is without essence, insubstantial, bereft of essence, and just as a setakaccha is without essence, insubstantial, bereft of essence, and just as a coral tree is without essence, insubstantial, bereft of essence, and just as a lump of foam is without essence, insubstantial, bereft of essence, and just as a bubble on the water is without essence, insubstantial, bereft of essence, and just as a mirage is without essence, insubstantial, bereft of essence, just as a banana trunk is without essence, insubstantial, bereft of essence, just as an illusion is without essence, insubstantial, bereft of essence—
cnd19:45.3: in just the same way form is without essence, insubstantial, bereft of essence, whether by way of the core essence of permanence, of pleasure, or of self, or by way of what is permanent, stable, eternal, or not liable to change.
cnd19:45.7: consciousness is without essence, insubstantial, bereft of essence, whether by way of the core essence of permanence, of pleasure, or of self, or by way of what is permanent, stable, eternal, or not liable to change.
cnd19:45.8: In this way he looks upon the world as empty by observing that choices are vacuous.
cnd19:45.9: He looks upon the world as empty for these two reasons.
cnd19:46.1: Furthermore, he looks upon the world as empty in six ways.
cnd19:46.2: The eye is empty of self or of what belongs to self, of the permanent, the stable, the eternal, or what is not subject to change,
cnd19:46.7: the mind is empty of self or of what belongs to self, of the permanent, the stable, the eternal, or what is not subject to change.
cnd19:46.13: Ideas are empty of self or of what belongs to self, of the permanent, the stable, the eternal, or what is not subject to change.
cnd19:46.27: Examination of ideas is empty of self or of what belongs to self, of the permanent, the stable, the eternal, or what is not subject to change.
cnd19:46.28: In this way he looks upon the world as empty in six ways.
cnd19:47.1: Furthermore, he looks upon the world as empty in ten ways.
cnd19:47.2: Form as hollow, as vacuous, as empty, as not-self, as without essence, as a killer, as non-existence, as the root of misery, as tainted, as conditioned;
cnd19:47.11: the round of transmigration as hollow, as vacuous, as empty, as not-self, as without essence, as a killer, as non-existence, as the root of misery, as tainted, as conditioned.
cnd19:47.12: In this way he looks upon the world as empty in ten ways.
cnd19:48.1: Furthermore, he looks upon the world as empty in twelve ways.
cnd19:48.2: Form is not a sentient being, not a soul, not a person, not a youth, not a woman, not a man, not self, not what belongs to self, not I, not mine, not anybody, not anybody’s;
cnd19:48.6: consciousness is not a sentient being, not a soul, not a person, not a youth, not a woman, not a man, not self, not what belongs to self, not I, not mine, not anybody, not anybody’s.
cnd19:48.7: In this way he looks upon the world as empty in twelve ways.
cnd19:49.2: “Mendicants, give up what is not yours.
cnd19:49.3: Giving it up will be for your lasting welfare and happiness.
cnd19:49.5: Form is not yours, mendicants; give it up.
cnd19:49.6: Giving it up will be for your lasting welfare and happiness.
cnd19:49.7: Feeling is not yours, mendicants; give it up.
cnd19:49.8: Giving it up will be for your lasting welfare and happiness.
cnd19:49.9: Perception is not yours, mendicants; give it up.
cnd19:49.10: Giving it up will be for your lasting welfare and happiness.
cnd19:49.11: Choices are not yours, mendicants; give them up.
cnd19:49.12: Giving them up will be for your lasting welfare and happiness.
cnd19:49.13: Consciousness is not yours, mendicants; give it up.
cnd19:49.14: Giving it up will be for your lasting welfare and happiness.
cnd19:49.15: Suppose, mendicants, a person were to carry off the grass, sticks, branches, and leaves in this Jeta’s Grove, or burn them, or do what they wish with them.
cnd19:49.17: ‘These people are carrying us off, burning us, or doing what they wish with us’?”
cnd19:49.20: “Because that, sir, is neither our self nor what belongs to our self.”
cnd19:49.21: “In the same way, mendicants, give up what is not yours;
cnd19:49.22: giving it up will be for your lasting welfare and happiness.
cnd19:49.24: Form is not yours, mendicants; give it up.
cnd19:49.25: Giving it up will be for your lasting welfare and happiness.
cnd19:49.29: consciousness is not yours, mendicants; give it up.
cnd19:49.30: Giving it up will be for your lasting welfare and happiness.”
cnd19:50.2: “‘The world is empty, the world is empty’, sir, they say.
cnd19:50.3: To what extent, sir, is it said that the world is empty?”
cnd19:50.4: “Because it is empty of self or of what belongs to self, Ānanda, it is said that the world is empty.
cnd19:50.5: And what, Ānanda, is empty of self or of what belongs to self?
cnd19:50.6: The eye, Ānanda, is empty of self or of what belongs to self.
cnd19:50.10: and the pleasant, painful, or neutral feeling that arises dependent on eye contact is also empty of self or of what belongs to self.
cnd19:50.23: and the empty feeling, pleasant, painful, or neutral, that arises dependent on mind contact is also empty of self or of what belongs to self.
cnd19:50.24: Because it is empty of self or of what belongs to self, Ānanda, it is said that the world is empty.”
cnd19:54.2: “In the same way, mendicants, a mendicant examines form as far as the range of form extends,
cnd19:54.3: examines feeling as far as the range of feeling extends,
cnd19:54.5: examines choices as far as the range of choices extends,
cnd19:54.6: examines consciousness as far as the range of consciousness extends.
cnd19:54.7: As they examine form as far as the range of form extends,
cnd19:54.11: as they examine consciousness as far as the range of consciousness extends, whatever notion of I, or mine, or I am they had, that too does not exist for them.”

cnd19:57.7: Any such view—a view, a viewpoint, a thicket of views, a desert of views, a twisting of views, a dodging of views, a fetter of views, a grasp, a clutching, an insistence, a misapprehension, a wrong path, a wrong way, wrongness, a sectarian ground, a perverted grasp, an inverted grasp, a distorted grasp, a wrong grasp, grasping the unreal as real, up to the sixty-two views—this is the theory of self.
cnd19:57.8: Having uprooted the theory of self: having uprooted it, having thoroughly uprooted it, having pulled it out, having thoroughly pulled it out, having torn it up, having thoroughly torn it up, having given it up, dispelled it, ended it, and brought it to non-existence—
